title_en: China Hengji Weiye Group Co., Ltd. and Beijing Beida Qingniao Co., Ltd. v. Guangsheng Investment Development Co., Ltd. and Hong Kong Qingniao Technology Development Co., Ltd. — dispute over loan guarantee contract
ruling_gist_en: Article 16 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of the Arbitration Law of the People's Republic of China provides: 'The validity of a foreign-related arbitration agreement shall be examined in accordance with the law chosen by the parties; if the parties have not chosen the applicable law but have agreed on the place of arbitration, the law of the place of arbitration shall apply; if the parties have neither chosen the applicable law nor agreed on the place of arbitration, or the agreement on the place of arbitration is unclear, the law of the forum shall apply.' Accordingly, in cases involving foreign-related contract disputes, where the parties have included an arbitration clause in the contract, they may simultaneously make a clear choice regarding the governing law for determining the validity of that arbitration clause. Due to the principle of independence of the arbitration clause, the governing law chosen in the contract for resolving the contract dispute cannot be used to determine the validity of the arbitration clause. If the parties have not chosen the governing law for determining the validity of the arbitration clause in the contract, nor agreed on the place of arbitration, or the agreement on the place of arbitration is unclear, the law of the forum shall apply to examine the validity of the arbitration agreement.

full_text_en:
China Hengji Weiye Group Co., Ltd. and Beijing Beida Qingniao Co., Ltd. v. Guangsheng Investment Development Co., Ltd. and Hong Kong Qingniao Technology Development Co., Ltd. — dispute over loan guarantee contract

Ruling Summary

Article 16 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Arbitration Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "The validity of a foreign-related arbitration agreement shall be examined in accordance with the law chosen by the parties; if the parties have not chosen the applicable law but have chosen the place of arbitration, the law of the place of arbitration shall apply; if the parties have neither chosen the applicable law nor the place of arbitration, or the place of arbitration is unclear, the law of the forum shall apply." Accordingly, in a foreign-related contract dispute, where the parties have included an arbitration clause in the contract, they may at the same time expressly agree on the governing law to determine the validity of that arbitration clause. Due to the principle of separability of an arbitration clause, the governing law agreed upon in the contract for resolving contractual disputes cannot be used to determine the validity of the arbitration clause. If the parties have not agreed in the contract on the governing law for determining the validity of the arbitration clause, and have also not agreed on the place of arbitration or the place of arbitration is unclear, the law of the forum shall apply to examine the validity of the arbitration agreement.

Civil Ruling of the Supreme People's Court

(2006) Min Si Zhong Zi No. 28

Appellant (Original Defendant): China Hengji Weiye Group Co., Ltd., domiciled at Room 1503, Sino Plaza, 255-257 Gloucester Road, Causeway Bay, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Legal Representative: Li Ming, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Yang Tiansheng, attorney at Beijing Mingtai Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Li Zhaoxia, employee of the company.

Appellant (Original Defendant): Beijing Beida Qingniao Co., Ltd., domiciled at Beida Qingniao Building, No. 207 Chengfu Road, Haidian District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Xu Zhendong, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Gao Yue, attorney at Beijing King & Wood Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Xu Guang, attorney at Beijing King & Wood Law Firm.

Appellee (Original Plaintiff): Guangsheng Investment Development Co., Ltd., domiciled at Room 1219, 12/F, Bank of America Tower, 12 Harcourt Road, Admiralty, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Legal Representative: Li Jinming, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Wang Hongxi, attorney at Beijing Deheng Law Firm Guangzhou Branch.

Agent ad litem: Zhou Linbin, attorney at Beijing Deheng Law Firm Guangzhou Branch.

Original Defendant: Hong Kong Qingniao Technology Development Co., Ltd., domiciled at Room 702, Asia Pacific Centre, 8 Wyndham Street, Central, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Legal Representative: Xu Zhendong, Director of the company.

Agent ad litem: Wang Fengli, attorney at Beijing King & Wood Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Jiang Shuo, attorney at Beijing King & Wood Law Firm.

The appellants, China Hengji Weiye Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Hengji Company) and Beijing Beida Qingniao Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Beijing Qingniao Company), in the case concerning the dispute over a loan and guarantee contract with Guangsheng Investment Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Guangsheng Company) and the original defendant, Hong Kong Qingniao Technology Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Hong Kong Qingniao Company), being dissatisfied with the civil ruling (2006) Yue Gao Fa Min Si Chu Zi No. 1 of the Guangdong High People's Court, appealed to this Court. This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law, with Judge Chen Bailing serving as the presiding judge, and Acting Judges Ren Xuefeng and Gao Xiaoli as members, to hear the case. Court Clerk Xu Yinglin served as the recorder. The trial of this case has now been concluded.

At the first instance, Guangsheng Company filed a lawsuit against Hengji Company, Hong Kong Qingniao Company, and Beijing Qingniao Company for repayment based on a loan contract dispute. Hengji Company and Beijing Qingniao Company raised objections to jurisdiction during the period for submitting their statements of defense, arguing that the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement contained an arbitration clause, thus the court had no jurisdiction, and requested dismissal of the lawsuit.

Upon examination, the court of first instance held that the main basis for Guangsheng Company's lawsuit in this case was the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement and its related guarantee agreements. Article 10 of the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement stipulated: "The four parties shall properly resolve any disputes arising during performance. If negotiations fail to resolve the dispute, it shall be submitted to arbitration for resolution. This agreement is governed by the laws of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China." This clause reflected the intention of the parties to submit disputes to arbitration and at the same time stipulated the governing law for resolving contractual disputes. However, since the parties did not stipulate the governing law for the validity of the arbitration clause, and also did not agree on the place of arbitration, the law of the place of arbitration could not be determined. Under these circumstances, the law of the forum, i.e., the mainland law of China, should be applied as the governing law for determining the validity of the arbitration clause. According to Article 16, paragraph 2 of the Arbitration Law of the People's Republic of China, an arbitration agreement must contain a designated arbitration commission. In the arbitration clause involved in this case, the parties only expressed their intention to arbitrate but did not specify a definite arbitration institution, nor did they reach a supplementary agreement on the arbitration institution. Pursuant to Article 18 of the Arbitration Law of the People's Republic of China, this arbitration clause should be deemed invalid. Since the arbitration clause is invalid, Guangsheng Company has the right to file a lawsuit with the court. Based on the claims of the parties and the main prima facie evidence, the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement is a bilateral contract, and the places where both parties perform their obligations can both be regarded as the place of contract performance. In this case, Guangsheng Company entrusted its affiliated company to transfer funds from a bank in Guangzhou to Hengji Company's affiliated company in Beijing. Therefore, Guangzhou should be one of the places of contract performance. By reference to Article 243 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court of first instance had jurisdiction over the dispute arising from the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement filed by Guangsheng Company against Hengji Company.

Hong Kong Qingniao Company and Beijing Qingniao Company provided guarantees to Guangsheng Company in connection with the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement. Therefore, the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement is the principal contract, and the guarantee agreements and guarantee letter are ancillary contracts. When Guangsheng Company files a lawsuit concerning both the principal and ancillary contracts, the jurisdiction over the ancillary contracts shall be determined in accordance with the principal contract. Since this court had jurisdiction over the dispute arising from the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement, it also had jurisdiction over the guarantee dispute filed by Guangsheng Company against Hong Kong Qingniao Company and Beijing Qingniao Company. In summary, the jurisdictional objections raised by Hengji Company and Beijing Qingniao Company were not well-founded and should be dismissed. Pursuant to Article 38 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this court ruled: The objections to jurisdiction over this case raised by Hengji Company and Beijing Qingniao Company are dismissed.

Hengji Company, dissatisfied with the above ruling of the court of first instance, appealed to this Court, arguing: 1. The first instance ruling was erroneous in determining the validity of the arbitration clause and the applicable law. The arbitration clause of the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement should be understood as a whole; any determination of the governing law for the content of this agreement, whether for resolving disputes or for determining the validity of the arbitration clause, should apply Hong Kong law. The arbitration clause is valid. 2. The first instance ruling's finding that Guangzhou was the place of contract performance was erroneous in fact. According to the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement, Guangsheng Company entrusted Guangdong Guangsheng Asset Management Co., Ltd. to perform its obligations, i.e., to pay RMB 100 million to Beijing Hengji Weiye Electronic Products Co., Ltd., which was entrusted by Hengji Company. Later, because Hengji Company failed to go public, the aforementioned sum was converted into a loan. The Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement did not specify the place of performance. Pursuant to Article 62 of the Contract Law, the place of performance should be the location of Beijing Hengji Weiye Electronic Products Co., Ltd., which was entrusted by Hengji Company to receive the payment, not the location of Guangsheng Company. 3. The first instance ruling applied the law incorrectly. Only on the premise of applying Article 62 of the Contract Law could this court "refer to" Article 243 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China to determine the competent court. In summary, the appellant requested that the ruling (2006) Yue Gao Fa Min Si Chu Zi No. 1 of the court of first instance be reversed and that Guangsheng Company's lawsuit be dismissed.

Beijing Qingniao Company, also dissatisfied with the above ruling of the court of first instance, appealed to this Court, arguing: 1. The court of first instance improperly applied the law. The Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement had already clearly stipulated the governing law, and this stipulation naturally extended to the arbitration clause. Moreover, all parties to the agreement were legal persons incorporated in Hong Kong. According to the principles of private international law, the governing law of the agreement should be determined by the national law of the parties. Therefore, the law applicable to the dispute in this case, including the determination of the validity of the arbitration clause, should be Hong Kong law. 2. The court of first instance did not clearly find the facts; the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement was not actually performed, so there was no place of performance. This case is a loan contract dispute. All parties to the contract are legal persons incorporated in Hong Kong, with their domiciles in Hong Kong. Pursuant to Article 18 of the Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, even if the arbitration clause is invalid, this case should be under the jurisdiction of the court of the defendant's domicile, that is, the Hong Kong court, not the court of first instance. The appellant requested that the civil ruling (2006) Yue Gao Fa Min Si Chu Zi No. 1 of the Guangdong High People's Court be reversed in accordance with the law and that the appellee's lawsuit be dismissed.

Guangsheng Company argued in defense: 1. The court of first instance correctly applied the law. The arbitration clause is independent, and the governing law for the arbitration clause is different from the governing law for the contract. 2. The contract has actually been performed. Guangzhou was the place of payment, which is one of the places of performance. The Guangdong High People's Court has legitimate jurisdiction. The relevant provisions of the Contract Law are not applicable to this case. 3. Beijing Qingniao Company, as a guarantor independent of the contract, has no right to raise objections to the jurisdiction arising from the principal contract.

Hong Kong Qingniao Company did not submit written legal opinions.

This Court finds: On December 25, 2002, Guangsheng Company, Hengji Company, Hong Kong Qingniao Company, and Dongying Asia Co., Ltd. entered into the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement. Article 10 of the agreement stipulated: "The four parties shall properly resolve any disputes arising during performance. If negotiations fail to resolve the dispute, it shall be submitted to arbitration for resolution. This agreement is governed by the laws of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China."

On December 25, 2002, Beijing Qingniao Company issued a Guarantee Letter to Guangsheng Company, the main content of which was to acknowledge the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement signed by its wholly-owned subsidiary, Hong Kong Qingniao Company, and to declare that it would assume joint and several liability for the guarantee obligations of Hong Kong Qingniao Company under the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement. This Guarantee Letter did not contain an arbitration clause.

This Court holds: In this case, the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement contains an arbitration clause and stipulates that "this agreement is governed by the laws of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China." Therefore, the governing law to be applied in examining the validity of the arbitration clause becomes the first issue to be considered in this case.

Article 16 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Arbitration Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "The validity of a foreign-related arbitration agreement shall be examined in accordance with the law chosen by the parties; if the parties have not chosen the applicable law but have chosen the place of arbitration, the law of the place of arbitration shall apply; if the parties have neither chosen the applicable law nor the place of arbitration, or the place of arbitration is unclear, the law of the forum shall apply." It follows that the parties may agree in the contract on the governing law for determining the validity of the arbitration clause, but such agreement must be explicit. The governing law agreed upon in the contract for resolving contractual disputes cannot be used to determine the validity of a foreign-related arbitration clause. In other words, the governing law applicable to the validity of the arbitration clause must be distinguished from the governing law applicable to the resolution of disputes. In this case, the stipulation under the arbitration clause that "this agreement is governed by the laws of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China" is ambiguous as to whether it is the governing law for the validity of the arbitration clause or the governing law for resolving contractual disputes, and cannot be deemed as an explicit agreement on the governing law for the validity of the arbitration clause. Since the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement does not stipulate the place of arbitration, the law of the forum, i.e., the mainland law of China, should be applied to determine the validity of the arbitration clause.

Article 18 of the Arbitration Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "If an arbitration agreement does not specify or clearly specify the matters for arbitration or the arbitration commission, the parties may reach a supplementary agreement; if they fail to reach such a supplementary agreement, the arbitration agreement is invalid." In this case, although the arbitration clause clearly expresses the intention to resolve disputes through arbitration, it does not designate an arbitration institution. The parties also failed to reach a supplementary agreement on the arbitration institution. Therefore, the arbitration clause should be deemed invalid, and the people's court has jurisdiction over this case. The finding of the court of first instance that the arbitration clause was invalid was correct.

Article 24 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "A lawsuit arising from a contract dispute shall be under the jurisdiction of the people's court of the place where the defendant is domiciled or where the contract is performed." Since the agreement involved in this case did not stipulate the place of performance, the actual place of performance should be used to determine jurisdiction.

Hengji Company and Guangsheng Company, as the issuer and buyer of the bonds under the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement, both confirmed the fact that Guangsheng Company had entrusted its affiliated company to pay funds to Hengji Company's affiliated company in Beijing, and acknowledged that the purpose of this act was to perform the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement. Although Beijing Qingniao Company argued that the payment was subject to China's foreign exchange control regulations, the funds paid could not be used to perform the agreement, and it had not received notice that the contract had been performed, so the agreement was not actually performed. However, whether a contract is performed is a question of fact, while whether the performance is appropriate and lawful pertains to the consequences and responsibilities of contract performance, which is a legal value judgment on legal facts and acts. Its claim that the contract was not performed cannot be upheld.

Article 62(3) of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "If the place of performance is unclear, and payment in currency is to be made, the place of performance shall be the place where the party receiving the currency is located." Based on the facts confirmed by the parties to the principal contract in this case, the party receiving the currency was Hengji Company's affiliated company in Beijing, namely Beijing Hengji Weiye Electronic Products Co., Ltd., whose domicile is in Beijing. Therefore, the place of performance of this contract should be determined as Beijing. The court of first instance's finding that Guangzhou was one of the places of performance and its conclusion based on this that the Guangdong High People's Court had jurisdiction over this case lacked factual and legal basis and should be corrected.

The amount of repayment claimed by Guangsheng Company in its lawsuit exceeds RMB 100 million. According to the case acceptance standards approved by the Supreme People's Court, the Beijing High People's Court has jurisdiction over the loan dispute filed by Guangsheng Company against Hengji Company and Hong Kong Qingniao Company.

Beijing Qingniao Company issued a Guarantee Letter to Guangsheng Company, undertaking to assume joint and several guarantee liability for the debts of Hong Kong Qingniao Company arising from the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement. Therefore, this Guarantee Letter should be an ancillary contract to the Convertible Bond Issuance Agreement. Since the Guarantee Letter does not contain an arbitration clause, and the domicile of Beijing Qingniao Company is in Beijing, and Guangsheng Company has sued both the principal debtor and the guarantor together, the Beijing High People's Court also has jurisdiction over this guarantee dispute.

In summary, the appellants' grounds of appeal are partially established, and this Court supports them. The ruling of the court of first instance on jurisdiction was improper and should be reversed. The Guangdong High People's Court shall transfer this case to the Beijing High People's Court for trial. Pursuant to Articles 24, 36, and 154 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 18 of the Arbitration Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 16 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Arbitration Law of the People's Republic of China, this Court rules as follows:

1. The civil ruling (2006) Yue Gao Fa Min Si Chu Zi No. 1 of the Guangdong High People's Court is reversed;

2. The Guangdong High People's Court shall transfer this case to the Beijing High People's Court for trial.

The case acceptance fee for the second instance, RMB 50, shall be borne by Guangsheng Investment Development Co., Ltd.

This ruling is final.

Presiding Judge: Chen Bailing
Acting Judge: Ren Xuefeng
Acting Judge: Gao Xiaoli

June 8, 2007

Court Clerk: Xu Yinglin
